text: The family brought in a turnaround manager named Poul Plougmann. The diagnosis sounded reasonable: children were changing faster than LEGO was. Maybe a box of bricks wasn't enough anymore.
So LEGO set out to become more than a brick company. Theme parks. Clothing. Video games. Television. And, for the first time, other people's worlds: Star Wars sets in 1999. Harry Potter in 2001.
At first, it looked brilliant. The Star Wars sets sold enormously. A new line of buildable warriors called Bionicle became a hit.
In 2001, LEGO also hired a young economist from McKinsey into its strategy department. His name was Jørgen Vig Knudstorp. For now, he was one person watching the plan from the inside.

And inside, the plan was creating something nobody saw on the shelves. Designers were free to invent. And much of what they invented was new pieces. A special piece for this set. A new color for that one.

Every new piece needs its own steel mold. Its own bin in the warehouse. Its own line in the factory schedule. In the late nineties, LEGO made about six thousand different elements. Within a few years, it was more than twelve thousand. And roughly nine out of ten new pieces were used in just one set.

Every one of those new pieces still clicked onto the old bricks. That was never the problem. The problem was that most of them were needed just once, and each one still had to be molded, stored and tracked.

Some new toys hardly needed building at all. Explore, a line for toddlers. Jack Stone, with big chunky parts that snapped together in minutes. And Galidor, a buildable action figure with its own TV show, video game and fast-food tie-in. It flopped.
Why didn't the numbers scream? Because of the movies. New Star Wars films came out in 1999 and 2002. Harry Potter in 2001 and 2002. Each one sold boxes of LEGO. And covered the cracks.
